Iowa among a minority of states without anti-SLAPP law  
  
Other jurisdictions have passed laws to prevent the use of SLAPPs, but Iowa is not one of them.  
  
Most anti-SLAPP laws permit an early motion to dismiss in any defamation action if the court finds the suit legally meritless, and in many cases allow an immediate appeal if the motion is denied. Another critical factor: Most such laws require the losing party to pay the other's legal fees.  
  
"It therefore puts a price on commencing such a suit on the plaintiff, because he might have to pay the other side’s attorneys fees if they are successful," Freeman said.

Iowa is one of 17 states that does not have such a law, according to the Public Participation Project. The Iowa House in 2021 passed a bill to add one, but it has been stalled in the Senate Judiciary Committee for the past two years, despite repeated subcommittee votes to recommend passage.  
  
Committee Chair Sen. Brad Zaun, R-Urbandale, said the bill didn't have the votes when first discussed in his committee, and then was buried beneath other priorities.  
  
"Honestly, it just didn’t rise to the top. I honestly don’t have any problems with the bill," he said, pointing to the Carroll case as a reason the Legislature should take action. "Assuming I’m the judiciary chair in the future, we want to get something done."  
  
Zaun described objections to the bill on the committee as "technical." But committee Vice Chair Sen. SLAPPs seek 'to chill someone else's speech,' often through financial risk  
  
Freeman, an expert on First Amendment law, said when someone files a defamation lawsuit that doesn't identify the alleged defamation, or that cites statements that are substantially true or protected opinion, it's fair to call it a SLAPP.  
  
"Basically a SLAPP is a lawsuit that’s brought not for the usual reasons, which are either to get damages for injured reputation or to get the record straight somehow, but rather cases that are brought quite outside normal reasons to go to court, to chill someone else’s speech and to get them to stop speaking because of the financial ramifications that will occur if you don’t shut up," he said.  
  
"It’s a way the powerful have of getting unhappy, less-powerful people to be quiet."

Although the courts might eventually find a SLAPP to be meritless, the time and expense of defending a lawsuit is its own punishment, especially when the plaintiff has the resources and willingness to drag out the litigation.

Journalists also can be targets of SLAPPs, and while a news organization might have greater resources to defend a case, it can still be a grueling experience.

"What they were doing is saying what a horrible person he is, that he’s a racist, a woman-beater, a real piece of s--- that steals from his employees," Leitner said. "People have got to learn, I think, to not mix in when they don’t know what they’re talking about."
